title: The cost of the Philippines' clan politics
gist: The Marcos-Duterte feud — Sara Duterte's impeachment trial, Rodrigo Duterte's ICC detention in The Hague and a gun-fired Senate standoff over fugitive senator Ronald dela Rosa — is a proxy war for the 2028 presidency, but the structural story is dynastic capture: 83 per cent of senators and 76 per cent of House members are dynasts, and a flood-control kickback scandal with losses possibly exceeding a trillion pesos (around £12 billion) shows the fiscal cost.

insights.claim: The 2022 'UniTeam' was a dynastic merger, not a party platform: Marcos Jr won the presidency with 58.8 per cent while Sara Duterte-Carpio took the separately elected vice-presidency with 61.5 per cent.
insights.speaker: Imran Shamsunahar
insights.so_what: Philippine electoral outcomes are best modelled as clan coalitions; alliance breakdowns, not policy shifts, drive political risk.
insights.locator: In May 2022, Ferdinand ‘Bongbong’ Marcos Jr

insights.claim: The alliance fractured first over Sara Duterte being given the education ministry rather than the more powerful defence ministry, then over the Marcos administration's greater alignment with the US versus the Dutertes' anti-Western stance, investigations into the drug war, and scandals implicating Duterte associates.
insights.speaker: Imran Shamsunahar
insights.so_what: The feud has an explicit foreign-policy axis: a Duterte restoration in 2028 would likely reverse the current US-aligned tilt in the South China Sea.
insights.locator: Relations between ‘Bongbong’ Marcos and Sara Duterte would deteriorate

insights.claim: Sara Duterte escalated in November 2024 by stating she had ordered a hit against Marcos Jr, his wife and the then-speaker of the House should anything befall her.
insights.speaker: Imran Shamsunahar
insights.so_what: Threats of this kind now form part of the formal impeachment charges — a reminder that elite conflict in Manila runs past institutional norms.
insights.locator: She courted further controversy in November 2024

insights.claim: Rodrigo Duterte, 81, was arrested in March 2025 and extradited to The Hague, where his ICC trial for crimes against humanity — murder, torture and rape during the anti-drugs campaign — is set to begin on 30 November, despite his having withdrawn the Philippines from ICC jurisdiction two years before the 2021 investigation opened.
insights.speaker: Imran Shamsunahar
insights.so_what: A 30 November trial date is a scheduled catalyst for Philippine political volatility ahead of the 2028 cycle.
insights.locator: in March 2025 the elder Duterte was suddenly arrested

insights.claim: Sara Duterte was impeached by an overwhelming House majority in May 2026 on charges of misused confidential funds, unexplained wealth and grave threats; a Senate conviction would bar her from office for life and destroy her 2028 presidential bid.
insights.speaker: Imran Shamsunahar
insights.so_what: The Senate verdict is the single binary event that determines the shape of the 2028 Philippine presidential field.
insights.locator: Matters escalated further in May this year

insights.claim: Sara Duterte remains the clear favourite to become the next president in almost all pre-election surveys carried out so far, while Marcos Jr is constitutionally barred from running again under the single six-year term limit.
insights.speaker: Imran Shamsunahar
insights.so_what: Absent conviction, the base case for 2028 is a Duterte presidency — with the associated tilt away from Washington.
insights.locator: In almost all pre-election surveys carried out so far

insights.claim: The conviction threshold itself is contested: the constitution requires votes from 'two-thirds of all the members' but the prosecution argues the threshold should count only senators able to actively take part in the trial.
insights.speaker: Imran Shamsunahar
insights.so_what: Arresting or sidelining hostile senators mechanically lowers the bar for conviction — a legal loophole with direct electoral consequences.
insights.quote: While the constitution states that a conviction requires votes from ‘two-thirds of all the members’, the prosecution has argued that the threshold should only include senators who can actively take part in the trial.
insights.locator: Whether this will have any bearing on its outcome

insights.claim: Senator-judges face crossed incentives: Duterte's continued public popularity argues for acquittal, while Marcos has dangled the vice-presidential position post-conviction as an inducement to convict.
insights.speaker: Imran Shamsunahar
insights.so_what: The vacated vice-presidency is the currency being used to buy the verdict — watch which senator accepts it.
insights.locator: For those senator-judges concerned about their future political career

insights.claim: Duterte-aligned senators briefly seized the Senate presidency on 11 May when Alan Peter Cayetano, Rodrigo Duterte's former foreign minister, was voted in by a slim majority of 13 in the 24-member chamber.
insights.speaker: Imran Shamsunahar
insights.so_what: Control of the Senate presidency is the operative control point over the impeachment trial — track defections vote by vote.
insights.locator: Those aligned with the Dutertes briefly seized control

insights.claim: The Duterte takeover hinged on the sudden reappearance of Senator Ronald dela Rosa — former national police chief and chief enforcer of the drug war — who had been in hiding since November 2025 under a since-unsealed ICC arrest warrant, and whose single vote tipped the chamber.
insights.speaker: Imran Shamsunahar
insights.so_what: Individual fugitive legislators can swing the balance of a 24-seat chamber — extreme sensitivity of outcomes to law-enforcement actions.
insights.quote: ‘encouraging the police to legitimise killings through fictitious self-defence scenarios, and promising impunity’
insights.locator: They have achieved this in part by the sudden and dramatic reappearance

insights.claim: A standoff inside the Senate ended with shots fired in the building, armed troops surrounding the premises and dela Rosa escaping, with Marcos' office disputing Senate security's account that National Bureau of Investigation personnel exchanged warning shots.
insights.speaker: Imran Shamsunahar
insights.so_what: Armed confrontation inside the legislature is a materially different risk regime than ordinary emerging-market political noise.
insights.locator: On the night of 14 July, things escalated dramatically

insights.claim: The Duterte Senate coup proved fleeting: on 17 June a Marcos-aligned senator ousted Cayetano, aided by a defection and by the absence of two Duterte-aligned senators — one in hiding, one arrested on 1 June over plunder charges tied to a bogus flood-control project.
insights.speaker: Imran Shamsunahar
insights.so_what: Corruption prosecutions are functioning as a vote-subtraction tool in the impeachment arithmetic.
insights.locator: The senate coup carried out by the Duterte camp proved fleeting

insights.claim: Sara Duterte has now lost three supposedly friendly senator-judges, with another allied senator arrested on plunder charges on the day of the trial.
insights.speaker: Imran Shamsunahar
insights.so_what: The acquittal math is deteriorating for the Dutertes in real time — a live count for anyone handicapping 2028.
insights.locator: The Dutertes’ position was further weakened

insights.claim: Dynastic control of Philippine politics is near-total: 83 per cent of current senators and 76 per cent of House members belong to dynasties, and 9,852 of 17,983 local elective posts — 54 per cent — are dynastic.
insights.speaker: Imran Shamsunahar
insights.so_what: Reform theses premised on electoral turnover misread the system; the binding constraint on Philippine governance is family control, not party competition.
insights.quote: According to one count, 83 per cent of current senators and 76 per cent of members of the House of Representatives belong to dynasties.
insights.locator: While political dynasties are a common phenomenon

insights.claim: Districts dominated by political dynasties show higher poverty and inequality and lower living standards than those with non-dynastic representatives.
insights.speaker: Imran Shamsunahar
insights.so_what: Dynastic concentration is a measurable drag on local development outcomes — a screening variable for regional investment exposure.
insights.locator: Research has found that districts dominated by political dynasties

insights.claim: Dynasties deter businesses and foreign investors by colluding with economic elites to block outside competition and capture extractive industries like mining, agriculture and forestry, with the need to connect to the right families acting as a major transaction cost.
insights.speaker: Imran Shamsunahar
insights.so_what: A concrete mechanism for the Philippines' chronic FDI underperformance versus regional peers, and one that does not respond to headline reform.
insights.locator: The presence of dynasties often serves to deter businesses

insights.claim: The dynasties' roots are colonial and pre-colonial: many families descend from mestizo landholders of the late Spanish period when common land was privatised and parcelled out to local elites, layered on indigenous tribal clan structures.
insights.speaker: Imran Shamsunahar
insights.so_what: Centuries-deep land-tenure origins imply this structure is not dislodgeable within an investment horizon.
insights.locator: Many of these dynastic families hail from the powerful mestizo landholders

insights.claim: The Marcos-Duterte rivalry maps onto the archipelago's geography, with the Marcos base in the far north of Luzon known as the Solid North and the Duterte base on Mindanao now called the Solid South.
insights.speaker: Imran Shamsunahar
insights.so_what: National contests resolve into two regional voting blocs — a simple heuristic for reading Philippine election polling.
insights.locator: In some sense, the rivalry between the Marcoses and the Dutertes

themes.theme: Pork barrel and the flood-control scandal

insights.claim: Pork barrel politics — distributing national budget funds to specific districts — is the executive's most important tool for pushing legislation through, and has long been criticised as a vehicle for corruption and patronage.
insights.speaker: Imran Shamsunahar
insights.so_what: Fiscal allocation in the Philippines follows coalition maintenance rather than project economics — discount announced infrastructure spend accordingly.
insights.locator: The realities of governing the Philippines require extensive bargaining

insights.claim: The flood-control kickback scandal — lawmakers, public works officials and contractors colluding on government-funded flood infrastructure — involves losses possibly exceeding a trillion pesos (around £12 billion), with an estimated 25 per cent of each project budget routinely skimmed.
insights.speaker: Imran Shamsunahar
insights.so_what: A 25 per cent standard leakage rate is a hard haircut to apply to Philippine public infrastructure spending forecasts.
insights.locator: Last year, an investigation revealed that lawmakers

insights.claim: Many flood-control projects were built with substandard materials or not built at all despite funds being disbursed, in a country that experiences close to 20 tropical cyclones a year.
insights.speaker: Imran Shamsunahar
insights.so_what: Physical climate risk in the Philippines is compounded by non-existent mitigation infrastructure — relevant to catastrophe insurance and sovereign risk pricing.
insights.locator: Many of the resultant projects were built with substandard materials

insights.claim: Legal exposure reaches the president's own family, with two members of Congress charged and three senators and eight congresspersons under investigation, including Marcos' cousin and former House Speaker Martin Romualdez.
insights.speaker: Imran Shamsunahar
insights.so_what: The anti-corruption drive cuts both ways and constrains how far Marcos can weaponise prosecutions against the Dutertes.
insights.locator: Among those charged in court are two members of Congress

insights.claim: The Marcos Sr dictatorship produced an estimated 3,257 extrajudicial killings, 35,000 cases of torture and 70,000 politically connected incarcerations, with Marcos, Imelda and cronies believed to have looted up to US$10 billion by 1986.
insights.speaker: Imran Shamsunahar
insights.so_what: Historical scale of elite extraction sets the reference point for what dynastic rule can cost a mid-sized economy.
insights.locator: Under the latter’s ‘New Society’ regime

insights.claim: Rodrigo Duterte's war on drugs is believed to have killed at least 5,000 and perhaps as many as 27,000 people, mostly small-time pushers from the urban poor, yet he left office hugely popular partly on his outsider status against the traditional elite of 'Imperial Manila'.
insights.speaker: Imran Shamsunahar
insights.so_what: Mass-casualty policy did not damage electability — a warning against assuming ICC prosecution will erode the Duterte brand at the polls.
insights.locator: As president, Duterte would become infamous

insights.claim: Whichever family wins, the corrosive dominance of political dynasties in Philippine politics is set to continue for the foreseeable future, so ordinary Filipinos pay the price either way.
insights.speaker: Imran Shamsunahar
insights.so_what: Do not trade the impeachment outcome as a governance-quality signal — the institutional cost structure is unchanged in either branch.
insights.quote: Regardless of which family comes out on top, the corrosive dominance of the political dynasties in the Philippines’ politics remains set to continue for the foreseeable future.
insights.locator: Regardless of which family comes out on top
